```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)
library(patchwork)
```

## **17.1 Introduction**

This chapter will focus on the lubridate package, which makes it easier to work with dates and times in R. We are going to focus on dates and date-times as R doesn’t have a native class for storing times. If you need one, you can use the **hms** package.

Dates and times are hard because they have to reconcile two physical phenomena (the rotation of the Earth and its orbit around the sun) with a whole raft of geopolitical phenomena including months, time zones, and DST.

- Most years have 365 days
- Leap years have 366
  - A year is a leap year if it’s divisible by 4, unless it’s also divisible by 100, except if it’s also divisible by 400. In other words, in every set of 400 years, there’s 97 leap years.
- Мost days have 24 hours
  - Places that use daylight saving time (DST), one day each year has 23 hours and another has 25

## **17.2 Creating date/times**

There are three types of date/time data that refer to an instant in time:

- A date. Tibbles print this as `<date>`.

- A time within a day. Tibbles print this as `<time>`.

- A date-time is a date plus a time: it uniquely identifies an instant in time (typically to the nearest second). Tibbles print this as `<dttm>`. Base R calls these POSIXct, but that doesn’t exactly trip off the tongue.

To get the current date or date-time you can use **today()** or **now()**:

```{r}

today()

now()
```

## During import

If your CSV contains an ISO8601 date or date-time, you don’t need to do anything; readr will automatically recognize it:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

csv <- 
  "date,datetime
  2022-01-02,2022-01-02 05:12"

read_csv(csv)
```

**ISO8601** - 2022-05-03 16:26 or 2022-05-03T16:26

{{< pagebreak >}}

All date formats understood by **readr**:

| Type  | Code  | Meaning                        | Example         |
|-------|-------|--------------------------------|-----------------|
| Year  | `%Y`  | 4 digit year                   | 2021            |
|       | `%y`  | 2 digit year                   | 21              |
| Month | `%m`  | Number                         | 2               |
|       | `%b`  | Abbreviated name               | Feb             |
|       | `%B`  | Full name                      | February        |
| Day   | `%d`  | One or two digits              | 2               |
|       | `%e`  | Two digits                     | 02              |
| Time  | `%H`  | 24-hour hour                   | 13              |
|       | `%I`  | 12-hour hour                   | 1               |
|       | `%p`  | AM/PM                          | pm              |
|       | `%M`  | Minutes                        | 35              |
|       | `%S`  | Seconds                        | 45              |
|       | `%OS` | Seconds with decimal component | 45.35           |
|       | `%Z`  | Time zone name                 | America/Chicago |
|       | `%z`  | Offset from UTC                | +0800           |
| Other | `%.`  | Skip one non-digit             | :               |
|       | `%*`  | Skip any number of non-digits  |                 |

А few options applied to a very ambiguous date:

```{r}

csv <- 
  "
    date
    01/02/15
  "

read_csv(
  csv, 
  col_types = cols(date = col_date("%m/%d/%y"))
)

read_csv(
  csv, 
  col_types = cols(date = col_date("%d/%m/%y"))
)

read_csv(
  csv, 
  col_types = cols(date = col_date("%y/%m/%d"))
)
```

If you’re using **`%b`** or **`%B`** and working with non-English dates, you’ll also need to provide a **locale()**.

See the list of built-in languages in **`date_names_langs()`**, or create your own with **`date_names()`**.

## From strings

lubridate’s helpers which attempt to automatically determine the format once you specify the order of the component. To use them, identify the order in which year, month, and day appear in your dates, then arrange “y”, “m”, and “d” in the same order:

```{r}

ymd("2017-01-31")

mdy("January 31st, 2017")

dmy("31-Jan-2017")
```

**ymd()** and friends create dates. To create a date-time, add an underscore and one or more of “h”, “m”, and “s” to the name of the parsing function:

```{r}

ymd_hms("2017-01-31 20:11:59")

mdy_hm("01/31/2017 08:01")
```

Force the creation of a date-time from a date by supplying a timezone:

```{r}

ymd("2017-01-31", tz = "UTC")
```

UTC timezone (also know as GMT, or Greenwich Mean Time, the time at 0° longitude) doesn’t use daylight saving time, making it a bit easier to compute with.

## From individual components

Instead of a single string, sometimes you’ll have the individual components of the date-time spread across multiple columns:

```{r}

flights |> 
  select(year, month, day, hour, minute)
```

Create a date/time from this sort of input: - **make_date()** for dates - **make_datetime()** for date-times:

```{r}

flights |> 
  select(year, month, day, hour, minute) |> 
  mutate(
    departure = make_datetime(year, month, day, hour, minute)
  )
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Apply to each of the four time columns in flights:

```{r}

make_datetime_100 <- 
  function(year, month, day, time) {
    make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100)
  }

flights_dt <- 
  flights |> 
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time)) |> 
  mutate(
    dep_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, dep_time),
    arr_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, arr_time),
    sched_dep_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, sched_dep_time),
    sched_arr_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, sched_arr_time)
  ) |> 
  select(origin, dest, ends_with("delay"), ends_with("time"))

flights_dt
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Distribution of departure times across the year:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

flights_dt |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = dep_time)
  ) + 
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 86400) # 86400 seconds = 1 day
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Or within a single day:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

flights_dt |> 
  filter(dep_time < ymd(20130102)) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = dep_time)
  ) + 
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 600) # 600 s = 10 minutes

```

Note that when you use date-times in a numeric context (like in a histogram), 1 means 1 second, so a binwidth of 86400 means one day. For dates, 1 means 1 day.

## From other types

Switch between a date-time and a date. That’s the job of **as_datetime()** and **as_date()**:

```{r}

as_datetime(today())

as_date(now())
```

*date/times* as numeric offsets from the “Unix Epoch”, 1970-01-01. - **as_datetime()** - if the offset is in seconds - **as_date()** - if it’s in days

```{r}

as_datetime(60 * 60 * 10)

as_date(365 * 10 + 2)
```

## Exercises

1.  What happens if you parse a string that contains invalid dates?

One gets parsed, and the other one throws an error, and is returned as NA

```{r}

ymd(c("2010-10-10", "bananas"))
```

2.  What does the **tzone** argument to `today()` do? Why is it important?

Sets the timezone. It's important because today might be a different date in different timezones.

3.  For each of the following date-times, show how you’d parse it using a readr column specification and a lubridate function.

```{r}

d1 <- 
  "January 1, 2010"

d2 <- 
  "2015-Mar-07"

d3 <- 
  "06-Jun-2017"

d4 <- 
  c("August 19 (2015)", "July 1 (2015)")

d5 <- 
  "12/30/14" # Dec 30, 2014

t1 <- 
  "1705" # gets parsed only with space between h & m

t2 <- 
  "11:15:10.12 PM"


```

**readr** column specifications:

```{r}
#| output: false

col_date(format = "%B %d, %Y")
col_date(format = "%Y-%b-%d")  
col_date(format = "%d-%b-%Y")
col_date(format = "%B %d (%Y)")
col_date(format = "%m/%d/%y")

col_time(format = "%H%M")
col_time(format = "%I:%M:%OS %p")
```

**lubridate** parsing

```{r}

mdy(d1)
ymd(d2)
dmy(d3)
mdy(d4)
mdy(d5)
hm("17 05")
hms(t2)
```

## **17.3 Date-time components**

This section will focus on the accessor functions that let you get and set individual components.

## Getting components

These are effectively the opposites of **make_datetime()**:

- **year()**
- **month()**
- **mday()** - day of the month
- **yday()** - day of the year
- **wday()** - day of the week
- **hour()**
- **minute()**
- **second()**

```{r}

datetime <- 
  ymd_hms("2026-07-08 12:34:56")

year(datetime)
month(datetime)
mday(datetime)

yday(datetime)
wday(datetime)

month(datetime, label = TRUE)
wday(datetime, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)

```

{{< pagebreak >}}

We can use wday() to see that more flights depart during the week than on the weekend:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

flights_dt |> 
  mutate(wday = wday(dep_time, label = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = wday)) +
  geom_bar()
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Average departure delay by minute within the hour.

There’s an interesting pattern: flights leaving in minutes 20-30 and 50-60 have much lower delays than the rest of the hour!

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

flights_dt |> 
  mutate(minute = minute(dep_time)) |> 
  group_by(minute) |> 
  summarize(
    avg_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = avg_delay)) +
  geom_line()
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Interestingly, if we look at the scheduled departure time we don’t see such a strong pattern:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

sched_dep <- 
  flights_dt |> 
  mutate(minute = minute(sched_dep_time)) |> 
  group_by(minute) |> 
  summarize(
    avg_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )

ggplot(
  sched_dep, 
  aes(x = minute, y = avg_delay)
) +
  geom_line()
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

So why do we see that pattern with the actual departure times?

Well, like much data collected by humans, there’s a strong bias towards flights leaving at “nice” departure times. Always be alert for this sort of pattern whenever you work with data that involves human judgement!

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

flights |>
  count(minute) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = n)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "minute", 
    y = "n", 
    title = str_wrap(
      "You can see a strong preference for round numbers like 0 and 30 and generally for numbers that are a multiple of five.", 
      width = 80
    )
  ) 
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Rounding

Round the date to a nearby unit of time, with **floor_date()**, **round_date()**, and **ceiling_date()**. Each function takes a vector of dates to adjust:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

flights_dt |> 
  count(week = floor_date(dep_time, "week")) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = week, y = n)
  ) +
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point()
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Use rounding to show the distribution of flights across the course of a day by computing the difference between dep_time and the earliest instant of that day:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

flights_dt |> 
  mutate(dep_hour = dep_time - floor_date(dep_time, "day")) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = dep_hour)
  ) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 60 * 30)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Computing the difference between a pair of date-times yields a difftime. We can convert that to an hms object to get a more useful x-axis:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

flights_dt |> 
  mutate(
    dep_hour = hms::as_hms(dep_time - floor_date(dep_time, "day"))
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = dep_hour)
  ) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 60 * 30)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Modifying components

Use each accessor function to modify the components of a date/time. This doesn’t come up much in data analysis, but can be useful when cleaning data that has clearly incorrect dates:

```{r}

(datetime <- 
   ymd_hms("2026-07-08 12:34:56"))


year(datetime) <- 2030

datetime

month(datetime) <- 01

datetime

hour(datetime) <- 
  hour(datetime) + 1

datetime

```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Alternatively, rather than modifying an existing variable, you can create a new date-time with update(). This also allows you to set multiple values in one step:

```{r}

update(
  datetime, 
  year = 2030, 
  month = 2, 
  mday = 2, 
  hour = 2
)
```

If values are too big, they will roll-over:

```{r}

update(
  ymd("2023-02-01"), 
  mday = 30
)

update(
  ymd("2023-02-01"), 
  hour = 400
)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Exercises

1.  How does the distribution of flight times within a day change over the course of the year?

The distribution of scheduled departure times is broadly stable throughout the year, with flights concentrated in the morning and late afternoon. Seasonal differences mainly affect the strength and sharpness of these peaks rather than their timing.

Morning departures peak around 06:00–09:00, with a sharper peak in January–March and September–December and a flatter pattern in summer. Counts dip around 10:00–13:00 before rising to a broader afternoon peak around 14:00–19:00. In July and August, morning and afternoon counts are more balanced.

Departures decline sharply after about 20:00 and remain uncommon overnight until roughly 05:00. There is no clear seasonal shift toward more overnight departures.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 12

flights |>
  mutate(
    departure_hour = hour + minute / 60,
    # R has a small number of built-in constants.
    # month.abb: the three-letter abbreviations for the English month names
    # Also: LETTERS, letters, month.name, pi
    month = factor(month, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = departure_hour)
  ) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 6),
    limits = c(0, 24)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Scheduled departure time (hour of day)",
    y = "Number of flights",
    title = "Scheduled departure times throughout the year"
  )
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

2.  Compare dep_time, sched_dep_time and dep_delay. Are they consistent? Explain your findings.

```{r}

comparison <- 
  flights |>
  filter(
    !is.na(dep_time),
    !is.na(sched_dep_time),
    !is.na(dep_delay)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    actual_departure = make_datetime(
      year, month, day,
      hour = dep_time %/% 100,
      min = dep_time %% 100
    ),

    scheduled_departure = make_datetime(
      year, month, day,
      hour = sched_dep_time %/% 100,
      min = sched_dep_time %% 100
    ),
    calculated_delay = as.numeric(
      difftime(actual_departure, scheduled_departure, units = "mins")
    ),

    difference = dep_delay - calculated_delay
  )

# Compare calculated and recorded delays
comparison |>
  count(difference, sort = TRUE)
```

A difference of 0 means the calculated delay matches dep_delay. Nonzero differences can arise because this code assigns both departure times the same date — even when the actual departure occurred after midnight on the following day. Constructing date - times from the flight date alone does not resolve that rollover.

Check whether all differences are whole - day offsets (it only checks that the discrepancies are multiples of one day):

```{r}

comparison |>
  summarise(
    day_offset =
      # all() combines the checks from near() into one result: 
      # TRUE if every check passes, or FALSE if at least one fails
      all(
        # near() checks whether each remainder is approximately zero
        near(
           # 1440 - the number of minutes in a day
          difference %% 1440, 0
        )
      )
  )
```

3.  Compare air_time with the duration between the departure and arrival. Explain your findings. (Hint: consider the location of the airport.)

`air_time` does not generally equal the difference between `arr_time` and `dep_time`. The main reasons could be time zones, departures or arrivals crossing midnight, and time spent on the ground. Departure and arrival times use each airport’s local time, while `air_time` measures minutes spent airborne.

```{r}


flights_airtime <-
  flights |>
  mutate(
    dep_time = (dep_time %/% 100 * 60 + dep_time %% 100) %% 1440,
    arr_time = (arr_time %/% 100 * 60 + arr_time %% 100) %% 1440,
    air_time_diff = air_time - arr_time + dep_time, 
    .before = 1
  ) |>
  filter(air_time_diff != 0) |>
  count()

flights_airtime
```

4.  How does the average delay time change over the course of a day? Should you use dep_time or sched_dep_time? Why?

Actual departure time (`dep_time`) is partly a consequence of delay. A flight scheduled for 18:00 but departing at 21:00 would be assigned to the 21:00 group if `dep_time` is used. That would move a delayed early-evening flight into a later group and distort the comparison of how punctual flights are at different scheduled times.

The broad finding is that earlier scheduled flights tend to have shorter average delays, while later flights tend to have longer delays.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

flights |>
  group_by(hour) |>
  summarise(
    avg_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_recorded = sum(!is.na(dep_delay)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = avg_delay)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 2)) +
  labs(
    x = "Scheduled departure hour",
    y = "Average departure delay (minutes)", 
    title = "Average departure delay by scheduled departure hour",
    subtitle = str_wrap(
      "Missing delays are excluded, so the plot does not measure the impact of cancellations", 
      width = 100
    )
  )
```

5.  On what day of the week should you leave if you want to minimise the chance of a delay?

```{r}

weekday_delays <- 
  flights |>
  mutate(
    date = make_date(year, month, day),
    weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1),
    delayed = dep_delay > 0
  ) |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  summarise(
    # fraction of flights that departed late
    proportion_delayed = mean(delayed, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_recorded = sum(!is.na(dep_delay)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

weekday_delays |>
  arrange(proportion_delayed)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot(
  weekday_delays, 
  aes(x = weekday, y = proportion_delayed)
) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(
    title = "Chance of a departure delay by weekday",
    x = "Day of the week",
    y = "Percentage of flights delayed"
  )
```

6.  What makes the distribution of `diamonds$carat` and `flights$sched_dep_time` similar?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

plot_1 <-
  ggplot(
    diamonds, 
    aes(carat)
  ) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 0.01
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.25)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3)) +
  labs(
    title = "Popular diamond weights",
    x = "Carat",
    y = "Number of diamonds"
  )

plot_2 <- 
  flights |>
  mutate(sched_min = sched_dep_time %% 100) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(sched_min)
  ) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 60, by = 5)) +
  labs(
    title = "Round scheduled departure times",
    x = "Scheduled departure minute",
    y = "Number of flights"
  )

plot_1 + plot_2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = str_wrap(
      "The shared feature is not the overall shape of the distributions, but the pronounced spikes at human-preferred values: human decisions influence both diamond weights and flight schedules.", 
      width = 120
    )
  )
```

Both distributions show many observations cluster at convenient, round values rather than being spread smoothly across nearby values.

`diamonds$carat` has spikes at popular weights, such as 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 carats. These reflect preferences for particular diamond sizes and incentives to produce diamonds at those weights.

`flights$sched_dep_time` clusters at round clock times, especially departures on the hour or half-hour, and more generally at five-minute intervals. Airlines choose these scheduled times rather than distributing departures evenly across every possible minute.

{{< pagebreak >}}

7.  Confirm our hypothesis that the early departures of flights in minutes 20-30 and 50-60 are caused by scheduled flights that leave early. Hint: create a binary variable that tells you whether or not a flight was delayed.

Large counts at scheduled minutes 30 and 0 show that many of these flights were scheduled for the half-hour or hour but departed a few minutes early.

```{r}

flights |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  mutate(
    dep_min = dep_time %% 100,
    sched_min = sched_dep_time %% 100,
    delayed = dep_delay > 0
  ) |>
  filter(
    # Strictly early
    dep_delay < 0,
    between(dep_min, 20, 29) |
      between(dep_min, 50, 59)
  ) |>
  count(sched_min, sort = TRUE)
```
{{< pagebreak >}}

## **17.4 Time spans**

Тhree important classes that represent time spans:

- **Durations** - represent an exact number of seconds

- **Periods** - represent human units like weeks and months

- **Intervals** - represent a starting and ending point

### **Durations**

In R, when you subtract two dates, you get a difftime object:

```{r}

# How old is Hadley?
h_age <- 
  today() - ymd("1979-10-14")

h_age
```

A difftime class object records a time span of seconds, minutes, hours, days, or weeks. Use **duration** from `lubridate` as an alternative:

```{r}

as.duration(h_age)
```

Durations come with a bunch of convenient constructors:

```{r}

dseconds(15)

dminutes(10)

dhours(c(12, 24))

ddays(0:5)

dweeks(3)

dyears(1)
```

Durations always record the time span in seconds. A year uses the “average” number of days in a year, i.e. 365.25. There’s no way to convert a month to a duration, because there’s just too much variation.

- Аdd and multiply durations:

```{r}

2 * dyears(1)

dyears(1) + dweeks(12) + dhours(15)
```

- Аdd and subtract durations to and from days:

```{r}

(tomorrow <- 
  today() + ddays(1))

(last_year <- 
  today() - dyears(1))
```

- Because durations represent an exact number of seconds, sometimes you might get an unexpected result:

```{r}

one_am <- 
  ymd_hms("2026-03-08 01:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")

one_am

one_am + ddays(1)
```

Why is one day after 1am March 8, 2am March 9? If you look carefully at the date you might also notice that the time zones have changed. March 8 only has 23 hours because it’s when DST starts, so if we add a full days worth of seconds we end up with a different time.

## Periods

To solve this problem, lubridate provides **periods**. Periods are time spans but don’t have a fixed length in seconds, instead they work with “human” times, like days and months:

```{r}

one_am

one_am + days(1)
```

- Periods can be created with a number of friendly constructor functions:

```{r}

hours(c(12, 24))

days(7)

months(1:6)
```

- Add and multiply periods:

```{r}

10 * (months(6) + days(1))

days(50) + hours(25) + minutes(2)
```

- Add them to dates. Compared to durations, periods are more likely to do what you expect:

```{r}

# A leap year
ymd("2024-01-01") + dyears(1)

ymd("2024-01-01") + years(1)

# Daylight saving time
one_am + ddays(1)

one_am + days(1)
```

Some planes appear to have arrived at their destination before they departed from New York City. Let's fix this:

```{r}

flights_dt |> 
  filter(arr_time < dep_time)
```
{{< pagebreak >}}

These are overnight flights. We used the same date information for both the departure and the arrival times, but these flights arrived on the following day. We can fix this by adding days(1) to the arrival time of each overnight flight:

```{r}

flights_dt <- 
  flights_dt |> 
  mutate(
    overnight = arr_time < dep_time,
    arr_time = arr_time + days(overnight),
    sched_arr_time = sched_arr_time + days(overnight)
  )

flights_dt |> 
  filter(arr_time < dep_time) 
```

## Intervals

- `dyears(1) / ddays(365) = 365.25 days` (dyears() is defined as the number of seconds per average year)

- `years(1) / days(1)` - depends on the year - 365 or 366

```{r}

years(1) / days(1)
```

- An **interval** is a pair of starting and ending date times, or you can think of it as a duration with a starting point. You can create an interval by writing **start %--% end**:

```{r}

y2023 <- 
  ymd("2023-01-01") %--% ymd("2024-01-01")

y2023

y2024 <- 
  ymd("2024-01-01") %--% ymd("2025-01-01")

y2024
```

- divide it by days() to find out how many days fit in the year:

```{r}

y2023 / days(1)

y2024 / days(1)
```

## Exercises

1.  Explain days(!overnight) and days(overnight) to someone who has just started learning R. What is the key fact you need to know?

overnight is TRUE for an overnight flight and FALSE otherwise. The ! symbol means “not”: it reverses TRUE and FALSE.

days() uses those values to create a period of one day or zero days.

The adjustment happens because TRUE acts like 1, and FALSE acts like 0 when used here. So days(overnight) becomes either days(1) or days(0)—one day or no days.

2.  Create a vector of dates giving the first day of every month in 2015. Create a vector of dates giving the first day of every month in the current year.

```{r}

(year_2015 <-
  make_date(year = 2015, month = 1:12, day = 1))

(current_year <-
  make_date(
    year = year(today()),
    month = 1:12,
    day = 1
  ))
  
```

3.  Write a function that given your birthday (as a date), returns how old you are in years.

```{r}

age <- 
  function(birthday) {
    floor(
      # computes the exact length of a time span
      # time_length(x, unit = "second")
      time_length(
        # interval() creates an Interval object with the specified start and end dates
        # interval(start = NULL, end = NULL, tzone = tz(start))
        interval(birthday, today()), 
        "years"
      )
    )
  }

birthday <- "2000-06-15"
  
age(birthday)
```

## **17.5 Time zones**

R uses the international standard IANA time zones. These use a consistent naming scheme `{area}/{location}`, typically in the form `{continent}/{city}` or `{ocean}/{city}`. Examples include “America/New_York”, “Europe/Paris”, and “Pacific/Auckland”.

- https://www.iana.org/time-zones

- what R thinks your current time zone is:

```{r}

Sys.timezone()
```

- Complete list of all time zone names:

```{r}

length(OlsonNames())

head(OlsonNames())
```

In R, the time zone is an attribute of the date-time that only controls printing. For example, these three objects represent the same instant in time.

- When creating a date-time, tz matters for interpreting the input. "12:00" in New York identifies a different moment from "12:00" in Copenhagen.

- Once the instant has been established, you can display it in another zone with `with_tz()` without changing the instant.

- `force_tz()` does something different: it keeps the clock reading but changes the zone, which changes the instant.

```{r}

x1 <- 
  ymd_hms("2024-06-01 12:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")
x1

x2 <- 
  ymd_hms("2024-06-01 18:00:00", tz = "Europe/Copenhagen")
x2

x3 <- 
  ymd_hms("2024-06-02 04:00:00", tz = "Pacific/Auckland")
x3
```

- verify that they’re the same time using subtraction or equality:

```{r}

x1 - x2
x1 - x3

x1 == x2
x2 == x3
```

```{r}

with_tz(x1, "UTC")

with_tz(x2, "UTC")

with_tz(x3, "UTC")
```

Unless otherwise specified, lubridate always uses UTC. It does not have DST, which makes a convenient representation for computation.

Operations that combine date-times, like c(), will often drop the time zone. In that case, the date-times will display in the time zone of the first element:

```{r}

x4 <- 
  c(x1, x2, x3)
x4
```

- times zones: they’re not all integer hour offsets!

- Change the underlying instant in time. Use this when you have an instant that has been labelled with the incorrect time zone, and you need to fix it:

```{r}

x4b <- 
  force_tz(x4, tzone = "Australia/Lord_Howe")
x4b

x4b - x4
```
